ground_truth.description: The init() function lacks access control and initialization guards, allowing repeated calls that overwrite the builderAdmin state variable. Attacker calls init(attacker_address) to seize admin, then sweep() to drain funds.
ground_truth.root_cause: The init() function lacks access control and initialization guards, allowing repeated calls that overwrite the builderAdmin state variable. Attacker calls init(attacker_address) to seize admin, then sweep() to drain funds.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: 1) Builder wallet deployed and accumulates fees. 2) Attacker calls init(attacker) to become admin. 3) Attacker calls sweep(token, attacker) to extract all balances.
ground_truth.fix_description: Implement access control on init() and add an initialization guard (require(!initialized)) to ensure single execution.

vulnerabilities.explanation: BuilderWallet is intended to be a fee recipient wallet whose admin (builderAdmin) is set by BuilderFactory right after deployment. However, init() is external and has no access control and no one-time initialization guard. Any address can call init() at any time and overwrite builderAdmin, permanently taking control of sweep(). This allows an attacker to steal all tokens that accrue to that BuilderWallet (e.g., builder fee splits routed to that deterministic address computed by RiskEngine). This exploit does not require compromising any trusted role.
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1) A BuilderWallet is deployed by BuilderFactory (or already exists) and is used as the fee recipient for a nonzero builderCode.
2) Fees/tokens accumulate in the BuilderWallet over time.
3) Attacker calls BuilderWallet.init(attackerEOA) to overwrite builderAdmin.
4) Attacker calls BuilderWallet.sweep(token, attackerEOA) to transfer the entire balance of any ERC20 held by the wallet to themselves.
5) Attacker can repeat sweep for all tokens and can re-init again if desired.

prediction.overall_explanation: RiskEngine is largely view/pure math and does not custody user funds, so most of its logic is not directly exploitable in isolation. The concrete exploitable issue is in the BuilderWallet fee-recipient subsystem: BuilderWallet.init() is publicly callable and re-initializable, allowing anyone to take over builderAdmin and steal all tokens sent to builder wallets. Other observed issues (e.g., event emission value in unlockPool) are not fund-loss vulnerabilities.
